cases.text: Open-loop action chunks preserve temporal structure but cannot respond to new contact signals during execution. Reactive Diffusion Policy (RDP) retains chunk-level sequence modeling while separating planning from feedback-conditioned action decoding. An action-only encoder compresses demonstration chunks, and a recurrent decoder learns to reconstruct actions from latent chunks and tactile or force observations. A diffusion planner predicts these latent chunks; during execution, the decoder incorporates the latest contact observation at each action update. TactAR supplies augmented-reality contact feedback during demonstration collection. Evaluations cover peeling, wiping, and bimanual lifting. Under post-contact disturbances, GelSight RDP achieves a demonstration-normalized peeling score of 0.80 versus 0.15 for tactile-input Diffusion Policy, supporting a control-architecture benefit beyond adding touch. The planner runs at 12 Hz and the decoder at 24 Hz; the tested feedback rate is constrained by GelSight's 25 Hz stream, and higher-rate operation remains untested.
cases.note: The draft left the link between latent chunks and fresh feedback implicit. Made the training-to-execution pathway explicit, retained the tactile-input comparator, and replaced a generic sensor limit with the tested rates.

cases.text: Under post-contact disturbances, GelSight RDP scored 0.80 on peeling versus 0.15 for tactile-input Diffusion Policy (Table II; ten trials per variation), comparing architectures while retaining tactile input. For post-contact-disturbance wiping (Table V), shortening the baseline's chunks from eight steps to two reduced grasp success from 100% to 20% and task score from 0.15 to 0.10. Eight-step temporal ensembling with factors 0.2 and 0.8 yielded grasp success of 30% and 100% and task scores of 0.05 and 0.15, respectively. Eight-step GelSight RDP achieved 100% grasp success and a 0.50 task score. Neither tested alternative matched this combination; these task-specific scores are not binary success rates.
cases.note: The draft omitted temporal ensembling and the matched wiping score. Centered the paragraph on post-contact controls, reporting both grasping and task scores to distinguish reactive performance from tactile availability or shorter chunks.

cases.text: Real-robot imitation learning faces costly demonstrations and simulation-to-real mismatch. This study co-trains Diffusion Policy on real demonstrations and task-aware digital cousins, independently developed simulation data, or both. Digital cousins preserve embodiment, action space, task goals and success criteria, and object and fixture categories, without requiring identical object instances or physical and visual properties. Task-aware demonstrations are generated by transforming and recombining object-centered trajectory segments. Across six real-world tasks on Panda and GR-1 robots, reported average success rates are 45.3% with real-only training, 81.1% with added digital cousins, 76.8% with added prior simulation, and 83.2% with both sources. Transfer depends on simulation sampling probability, not just dataset size, and benefits from approximate camera alignment despite mismatched camera models. Prior Panda data also undergo camera re-rendering; the findings therefore do not establish transfer from entirely unmodified simulation data.
cases.note: The draft reported only the combined-data gain and left permissible mismatches underspecified. Added separate simulation-source comparisons, completed the digital-cousin definition, and retained sampling, approximate alignment, and prior-data re-rendering conditions.

cases.text: Co-training raised reported average success across six tasks from 45.3% with real-only training to 81.1% with digital cousins, 76.8% with prior simulation, and 83.2% with both (Table I). With CupPnP datasets fixed at 20 real and 1,000 simulated demonstrations, success reached 85% at 50% simulation sampling and 95% at 90% or 99%, but fell to 60% at 99.9% (Figure 5). Replacing approximately aligned simulation-camera views with default unaligned views reduced digital-cousin co-training success from 67% to 56% on CounterToSinkPnP and from 95% to 70% on CupPnP (Figure 6). The aligned humanoid camera still omitted real fisheye distortion: approximate alignment helped without identical camera models.
cases.note: The draft listed outcomes without fully connecting the controls to transfer conditions. Organized fixed-dataset sampling results around their nonmonotonic trend and contrasted approximate alignment with default views while preserving the camera-model mismatch.

cases.text: Hand occlusion can erase object geometry from single-view RGB-D point clouds. CordViP samples an image-generated object model, transforms its point cloud using FoundationPose estimates, and obtains hand geometry through forward kinematics. Geometry beyond visible depth points is thus available under partial occlusion, provided the object model is accurate and pose tracking continues. Play-data pretraining predicts geometrically derived contact maps and reconstructs arm actions from hand state and hand actions from arm state, with point clouds conditioning both reconstructions. A diffusion policy then learns action sequences while fine-tuning the pretrained encoder. With 50 expert demonstrations per task in addition to pretraining, CordViP achieves 90% average success across four base tasks versus 74% for pose-informed G3Flow. Removing both pretraining objectives while retaining the representation yields 79%, supporting a benefit beyond cleaner point clouds. Complete occlusion can still break tracking, and deformable objects challenge the rigid-pose representation.
cases.note: The draft left contact supervision and the coordination operation implicit. Explained geometry-based pretraining, linked model geometry to continued tracking, and retained a pose-informed comparator plus the fixed-representation ablation to separate learning benefits from observation quality.

cases.text: Following separate pretraining and 50 expert demonstrations per task, CordViP averaged 90% success across four base tasks evaluated with 20 trials each, versus 74% for pose-informed G3Flow and 23% for RGB-D-derived DP3 (Table I). Supplying interaction-aware point clouds to DP3 yielded 71%, but this comparison changes the representation. With CordViP's representation fixed, removing both pretraining objectives yielded 79%; removing contact or coordination alone yielded 84% or 83%, respectively (Table VII). These ablations support benefits from both learning objectives beyond the observation representation. Viewpoint tests used recalibrated cameras, and complete object occlusion can still break pose tracking despite robustness under partial occlusion.
cases.note: The draft listed ablations without specifying what stayed fixed. Distinguished the pose-informed comparison, representation substitution, and fixed-representation pretraining controls, while retaining separate pretraining data, camera recalibration, and the complete-occlusion boundary.
